somalia.content: Somalia President Rules Out Role in Ethiopia-Eritrea War | Kulu Media Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Connect with us Search Kulu Media Somalia Will Stay Out of Ethiopia-Eritrea Conflict, President Says Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Home » Politics » Somalia Will Stay Out of Ethiopia-Eritrea Conflict, President Says Politics Somalia Will Stay Out of Ethiopia-Eritrea Conflict, President Says Somalia’s president says his country will stay out of any Ethiopia-Eritrea conflict while addressing Red Sea security, Somaliland and foreign military bases. Published 50 seconds ago on October 30, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud speaks during an interview with Sky News about regional security, Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions and Somalia's foreign policy. Credit: Sky News / Screenshot Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has said his country will not participate in any conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea, reaffirming Mogadishu’s commitment to regional neutrality while rejecting foreign military arrangements that could turn Somalia into a base for proxy confrontations. In an extensive interview with Sky News , Mohamud discussed rising tensions across the Horn of Africa, relations with Ethiopia and Eritrea, security in the Red Sea, the fight against Al-Shabaab and the dispute over Somaliland. Asked how Somalia would respond to a possible war between Ethiopia and Eritrea, the president said his government maintained good relations with both countries and had no intention of becoming involved in their disputes. “Somalia is not going to participate any conflict at all,” Mohamud said, stressing that Mogadishu would not interfere in the internal affairs of other countries. He added that Somalia’s foreign policy was guided by the principle of maintaining peace domestically and with the international community. His remarks reinforce Somalia’s previous declaration of neutrality amid the escalating confrontation between Addis Ababa and Asmara. Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated significantly in recent weeks, with both governments exchanging accusations over military activities, territorial security and alleged support for armed groups. The two countries severed diplomatic relations earlier this month, raising concerns that renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia could develop into a broader regional conflict. Mohamud emphasized that Somalia was primarily focused on its own security challenges rather than becoming involved in disputes beyond its borders. He said the African Union security mission in Somalia had been reduced from more than 20,000 personnel to approximately 11,000 as Somali forces gradually assumed greater responsibility for national security. The president acknowledged the contributions of Ethiopia, Kenya, Djibouti, Uganda and Burundi to Somalia’s security efforts. Somalia Rejects Foreign Proxy Bases Turning to competition for influence in the Red Sea, Mohamud rejected the possibility of allowing foreign countries to establish military facilities intended to support proxy conflicts. “We will never have given any opportunity for the countries that wanted to establish a proxy basis in our country,” he said. Asked specifically about the United Arab Emirates, the president said Somalia’s previous defence and security agreement with Abu Dhabi had been cancelled. He argued that activities conducted by the UAE inside Somalia without federal authorization were illegal. The interview did not provide details about the cancellation’s date, the specific agreements affected or the UAE’s response to the president’s latest remarks. Mohamud also expressed concern about the growing competition among international and regional powers seeking strategic influence around the Red Sea. He identified piracy and the conflict in Yemen as two major challenges affecting maritime security. The president argued that military operations alone could not eliminate piracy because armed groups operate from communities on land. He called for stronger coastal security, economic opportunities and international assistance to help Somalia protect its approximately 3,400-kilometre coastline. President Accuses Israel of Seeking Naval Base in Somaliland Mohamud also accused Israel of pursuing strategic military interests in Somaliland, the self-declared republic that seeks international recognition as an independent state. Asked why Israel had recognized Somaliland, the president claimed the decision was motivated by a desire to establish a naval presence near the Red Sea. “All they want is to have a naval base in that area,” he said. He argued that Israel’s interest was driven by military considerations rather than support for Somaliland’s political aspirations or economic development. The president did not present evidence in the interview establishing a finalized Israeli naval-base agreement. His comments should therefore be understood as the Somali government’s assessment of Israel’s intentions, not independent confirmation that such a base has been agreed upon or established. Mohamud reiterated that his government opposed Somaliland’s separation from Somalia and remained committed to the country’s territorial unity. He said Somalia continued to seek dialogue with Somaliland’s leadership, while maintaining that the situations in Puntland and Jubaland were different because those federal member states did not seek independence. The president also expressed confidence that the United States would maintain its longstanding recognition of Somalia’s territorial integrity despite Somaliland’s efforts to secure American diplomatic recognition. Mohamud Says Somalia Is Winning War Against Al-Shabaab Addressing domestic security, Mohamud rejected suggestions that territorial losses to Al-Shabaab meant Somalia was losing its campaign against the militant group. He acknowledged that government forces had lost control of some areas after military advances beginning in 2022 but said only two previously liberated districts had been retaken by the militants. That territorial assessment was the president’s claim and was not independently verified in the interview. Mohamud argued that Al-Shabaab had become weaker than it was four or five years earlier, citing losses among its leadership and reductions in territory under its control. He described the government’s strategy as combining military operations with ideological efforts and measures to disrupt the group’s financing. The president also warned that youth unemployment and poverty continued to make young Somalis vulnerable to recruitment. He said Al-Shabaab offered some recruits monthly payments as low as $30 for unmarried members and $70 for married members, illustrating the economic hardship that militant groups could exploit. Youth Employment and Humanitarian Aid Remain Major Challenges Mohamud identified Somalia’s young population as one of the most important challenges facing his government. He said more than 70 percent of Somalis were under 30 and warned that failing to provide education and employment opportunities could create further instability. The president highlighted efforts to expand public education, provide microfinance and support businesses established by young entrepreneurs. He acknowledged that the government’s ambition to bring three million students into education had not yet been achieved. Mohamud also criticized aspects of the international humanitarian aid system, arguing that long-term reliance on assistance could undermine economic independence. He called for greater investment in farming, vocational training and employment opportunities rather than concentrating exclusively on recurring financial and food assistance. His comments came as Sky News highlighted the impact of humanitarian funding shortages on health clinics and nutrition services. The president acknowledged that climate shocks, droughts and flooding were placing additional pressure on Somali communities. He also said international financial support should better reflect priorities identified by Somalia itself. Regional Neutrality Amid Growing Security Pressures Mohamud’s statements come at a sensitive moment for the Horn of Africa, where tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have intensified alongside renewed conflict in northern Ethiopia. The two countries have exchanged accusations concerning armed groups and military threats, while international governments have called for diplomatic restraint . Somalia has sought to maintain working relations with both countries despite broader regional disagreements. Mohamud previously said Mogadishu was also prepared to discuss Ethiopia’s access to the sea through negotiated arrangements respecting Somalia’s sovereignty. His latest interview reinforces that position while drawing a clear distinction between bilateral cooperation and participation in another country’s military confrontation. The president presented Somalia’s priorities as strengthening domestic security, reducing dependence on international assistance, creating economic opportunities for young people and preventing foreign rivalries from further destabilizing the country. Addressing the Third Russia–Africa Summit in Moscow, Abiy said the proposed Ethiopia nuclear power plant would diversify the country’s electricity supply, which currently relies heavily on hydropower. “With Russia, we are moving toward our first nuclear power plant in line with the safety standards of the International Atomic Energy Agency,” Abiy said in his summit speech , published on his official YouTube channel. The prime minister said nuclear technology could also help reduce agricultural food losses and support healthcare, including cancer treatment. He emphasized that cooperation with Moscow should develop Ethiopian expertise to operate and regulate nuclear facilities. The remarks come as Ethiopia seeks to diversify its electricity generation beyond hydropower, which remains vulnerable to variations in rainfall and reservoir inflows. Earlier this year, Ethiopian Electric Power reported a 20 percent reduction in water inflows linked to El Niño conditions, prompting revisions to its electricity generation and revenue targets. Ethiopia’s nuclear ambitions have been under development for several years. The country signed an intergovernmental nuclear cooperation agreement with Russia in 2019, followed by additional cooperation roadmaps. In March 2026, the Ethiopian Nuclear Energy Commission and Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom signed a strategic roadmap covering nuclear energy development. According to World Nuclear News, Ethiopia is considering two reactors with a combined generating capacity of approximately 2,400 megawatts. However, the project remains at the planning stage, with potential sites requiring further assessment. Abiy did not announce a construction start date, final financing agreement or completion timetable during his Moscow address. The prime minister identified food security, energy and knowledge as Ethiopia’s three principal development priorities. On agriculture, he called for Russian cooperation in farm machinery and agricultural processing industries to increase domestic production and strengthen food security. He said Ethiopia wanted to move beyond producing raw agricultural commodities by expanding industries capable of processing harvested products. Abiy also announced that Ethiopia is establishing the Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa and invited Russian universities and research institutions to participate in teaching and research. “An African researcher should be able to create tools in the language of our people,” he said, emphasizing that African institutions should determine how artificial intelligence systems use their data. The proposed university forms part of Ethiopia’s broader technological development ambitions. At the recent Tana High-Level Forum, Abiy also outlined the country’s Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy , highlighting digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and data governance as priorities for economic development. The prime minister said scientific cooperation should produce practical economic benefits rather than remain limited to academic exchanges. He invited Russian enterprises to establish joint ventures in Ethiopia’s special economic zones, particularly in pharmaceutical manufacturing and machinery production. Such investments, he said, could supply markets across Africa through the African Continental Free Trade Area. Abiy also called for improved payment arrangements between Ethiopia and Russia to make bilateral trade simpler and less expensive. His proposals came as the two countries continued expanding diplomatic, economic and military cooperation. During the Moscow summit, Abiy held bilateral discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin on nuclear energy, healthcare, trade and other areas of mutual interest. The talks followed Ethiopia’s recent announcement concerning the acquisition of Russian military aircraft and air-defence equipment. On October 28, Kulu Media reported that Ethiopia announced new Russian Su-35 fighter jets amid renewed military tensions in the Horn of Africa. The latest summit discussions indicate that Ethiopia is seeking cooperation with Moscow across both civilian and defence sectors. Abiy also proposed that Addis Ababa host a future Russia–Africa Summit when the gathering next takes place on the African continent. He said the Ethiopian capital, which hosts the African Union headquarters, would be honored to welcome the meeting. However, he did not announce that Addis Ababa had been formally selected as the venue. The prime minister urged participating countries to adopt an action plan containing clear responsibilities and implementation timelines. He said international cooperation should translate diplomatic commitments into practical results. On international affairs, Abiy reaffirmed Ethiopia’s support for negotiated solutions, African-led mediation and consistent application of the United Nations Charter. His remarks came amid continuing Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions , with international partners urging restraint and diplomatic engagement to prevent a broader regional conflict. Abiy did not directly address the dispute with Eritrea in the supplied summit speech. Reflecting on historical relations, the prime minister recalled a Russian medical mission that assisted wounded Ethiopians following the Battle of Adwa in 1896. He said the mission translated a medical guide into Amharic, presenting the initiative as an early example of scientific cooperation between the two countries. Abiy also noted that his book Medemer had been translated into Russian, describing the exchange of knowledge as a symbol of the longstanding relationship. The speech concluded with a call for stronger cooperation based on sovereignty, technological capability and shared economic development. For Ethiopia, the proposed nuclear power plant, artificial intelligence university and expanded industrial partnerships represent central elements of the government’s long-term development agenda. However, the financing, construction timetable and implementation arrangements for the nuclear project remain to be finalized. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search Featured Somalia: Three Strategic Shifts, One Unchanged Political Mindset Posted by: Horseed Staff As insurgents adapt and regional powers recalculate, Somalia’s political elite remains trapped in struggles that leave the country vulnerable. 30 October, 2026 Share Tweet By: MP Abdirahman Abdishakur Warsame A nation’s direction is shaped by the outlook, character and conduct of its elite, particularly those entrusted with political leadership. Through the priorities they set and the public discourse they shape, leaders influence how citizens understand domestic challenges and international threats. Whether a country navigates upheaval or is overwhelmed by it depends in large measure on their ability to recognise danger, adapt to changing circumstances and place national interests above personal ambition. When their thinking remains fixed while the world around them changes, the consequences extend far beyond their own political fortunes. Somalia faces precisely this challenge. Al-Shabaab appears to be adapting its tactics, regional powers are recalculating their interests, and a weakening international order creates greater room for interference. Yet Somali politicians remain absorbed in familiar struggles over office, clan influence and control of institutions. The government explains the crisis through accusations of betrayal, alleging cooperation between forces loyal to the ousted South West administration and Al-Shabaab, while portraying political opponents as serving foreign interests. Credible allegations require investigation, but they do not absolve the government of responsibility for decisions that have made Somalia vulnerable. The central danger does not require a predetermined conspiracy, it emerges when political exclusion creates a crisis that different actors exploit for separate purposes. The political settlement being dismantled Somalia’s political settlement rested on federalism, a parliamentary system, elections every four years and power-sharing. Although imperfect and frequently contested, these arrangements provided guarantees through which a fragmented country could rebuild common institutions while protecting the participation and representation of its constituent communities. The settlement also depended on compromise, consensus-building and shared leadership, because no single actor possessed sufficient authority or legitimacy to determine the country’s direction alone. A common national agenda therefore had to be negotiated. Hassan Sheikh’s approach has undermined both the settlement’s foundations and the practices that sustained it. The direction is towards centralisation rather than federal accommodation, presidential dominance rather than parliamentary accountability, mandate extension rather than predictable elections, and concentrated authority rather than negotiated power-sharing. The accompanying attitude is captured by “loo joojin maayo” “ We will proceed regardless of objections” , and “talo dhexda la dhigayo ma jirto”—“decisions are not open to collective deliberation.” These expressions convey an approach in which consultation gives way to instruction, and agreement is replaced by an expectation of compliance. What should be a negotiated national undertaking becomes a presidential project that others are expected to accept. The dispute consequently extends beyond personal rivalry: when the rules governing representation, authority and succession are changed unilaterally, confidence in political participation itself begins to collapse. Exclusion has created strategic vulnerability By dismantling the political settlement and combining transactional politics with intimidation reinforced by foreign backing, the federal leadership has left its opponents feeling threatened, humiliated and politically subjugated. As confidence in institutions’ ability to protect their interests and resolve disputes has eroded, they have begun seeking guarantees outside those institutions. Political rivals view exclusion as a threat to their survival, while communities interpret struggles over authority as threats to their collective security. Consequently, disputes that could have been resolved through negotiation have created openings for armed mobilisation and external involvement. These outcomes are not inevitable, but they are foreseeable when negotiated safeguards are dismantled without an agreed alternative. The government bears primary responsibility for preventing this deterioration because it controls federal institutions. Its opponents remain accountable for their choices, but government policy must also be judged by the reactions it encourages and the vulnerabilities it creates. Three strategic shifts make those vulnerabilities especially dangerous. First: insurgents adapt to political grievances Al-Shabaab appears to be exploiting political fractures through greater tactical flexibility. The accommodation with forces associated with displaced administrations and aggrieved clans could provide political cover, soften clan resistance and complicate international scrutiny by blurring the distinction between insurgency and local political confrontation. Such flexibility should not be confused with moderation, because temporary accommodation can advance an insurgent project without changing its objectives. Whereas a displaced leader may seek to recover office and a clan may seek protection, Al-Shabaab can exploit the same confrontation to expand its presence and weaken resistance to its authority. The consequences may therefore outlast the arrangement: actors seeking immediate leverage could help establish an insurgent foothold that they cannot subsequently remove. No political grievance justifies cooperation with Al-Shabaab. Nevertheless, condemning such cooperation, where substantiated, cannot substitute for addressing the exclusion that weakens collective resistance to insurgency. Second: regional powers exploit the fractures Regional powers may find opportunities in the same instability, although their objectives differ: one may seek to preserve a local partner, another to weaken a geopolitical rival, and another to erode Somali sovereignty by deepening fragmentation and limiting the country’s ability to act independently. As Somali actors seek external backing, domestic confrontations become entangled with competition across the Horn of Africa, the Red Sea and the Middle East. Where states tolerate or indirectly exploit insurgent activity against an adversary, counterterrorism commitments risk becoming subordinate to strategic advantage. Such accommodation need not involve a formal alliance to cause harm, although overlapping interests alone do not establish coordination. Foreign governments remain responsible for interference, but Somali leaders must anticipate their calculations. An administration cannot alienate domestic constituencies and then treat their search for outside support as wholly unexpected; equally, its opponents cannot invoke exclusion to justify compromising national sovereignty Third: international restraints are weakening The fragmentation of the international order compounds these threats, as selective enforcement of international norms gives middle powers greater room to pursue influence through local partners and proxies. Although sovereignty and territorial integrity remain fundamental rights, their practical protection becomes less dependable when international institutions struggle to restrain interference. Domestic cohesion consequently acquires greater strategic importance. Political confrontation weakens security cooperation, insecurity increases dependence on foreign support, and dependence gives external actors greater leverage over decisions that should belong to Somalis. The responsibility to change course rests with the federal leadership The danger is a convergence in which politicians seek power, insurgents seek expansion and regional actors seek strategic advantage. Their actions can reinforce one another without a shared ideology or coordinated plan, producing consequences far beyond any actor’s immediate intentions. The responsibility for breaking this cycle rests, above all, with Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. He must recognise the magnitude of the challenges, acknowledge the limits of his power and judgment, and take responsibility for the consequences of his unilateral decisions. Doing so requires the humility to admit mistakes and the resolve to change course. His determination to remain in office must yield to his duty to protect the country. Credible, good-faith negotiations on the electoral process and a peaceful transfer of power must begin immediately, accompanied by concrete steps to rebuild confidence and halt unilateral actions that deepen mistrust. Political grievances cannot be resolved through coercion; they require genuine dialogue, mutual assurances and a willingness to reach meaningful compromises. Security institutions must serve the nation rather than partisan interests, while foreign partnerships must be transparent, accountable and consistent with Somalia’s sovereignty. Somali leaders must come together to assess the changing strategic environment and agree on a common national response that places the country’s security and independence above their competing ambitions. Above all, the federal leadership must recognise that domestic political agreement is a foundation of sovereignty. Unless it changes course, its determination to retain control of the state may undermine Somalia’s ability to determine its own future. somalia.summary: Somalia is facing significant challenges as its political elite remains entrenched in power struggles, leaving the country vulnerable to insurgent threats and regional interference. Despite Al-Shabaab adapting its tactics and regional powers recalibrating their interests, Somali leaders are preoccupied with clan influence and institutional control. The current administration, led by Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, is accused of undermining the foundational political settlement based on federalism and power-sharing, opting instead for centralization and unilateral decision-making. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Somalia repatriates 169 citizens from Libyan prisons Posted by: Horseed Staff Somalia has repatriated 169 of its citizens who were being held in prisons in Libya, according to the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. 30 October, 2026 Share Tweet The returnees arrived in Somalia through the Voluntary Humanitarian Return programme, with 140 landing in Mogadishu and a further 29 travelling to Hargeisa. The programme is supported by the European Union in Somalia and implemented by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in coordination with the Somali federal government. The IOM described the operation as a “safe and dignified return”, giving the returnees an opportunity to reunite with their families and begin rebuilding their lives. Ibrahim Guure, director of the diaspora and communities department at Somalia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, was among officials who received the returnees in Mogadishu. The latest repatriation comes as Somali authorities and international organisations continue efforts to address irregular migration, particularly among young people. A separate discussion on preventing irregular migration among young Somalis was also held in Mogadishu, attended by Prof Mohamed Omar Dhalxa and representatives of youth organisations. More returns from Libya The latest operation is part of a series of IOM-supported returns of Somali migrants from Libya. In September, 171 Somali migrants stranded in Libya were assisted in returning home on an IOM charter flight. Forty-two disembarked in Hargeisa, while the remainder travelled to Mogadishu. Some of those returnees, including three minors, had travelled through several countries before experiencing exploitation and abuse by smugglers in Libya. In July, Somalia’s National Commission for Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons provided immediate assistance to nearly 130 Somali nationals repatriated from Libyan detention centres. The assistance included medical examinations, registration with the National Identification and Registration Authority and support to reunite returnees with their families. Earlier, in April, 174 Somali citizens were repatriated from Libya, with Deputy Foreign Minister Hassan Mohamed Ali among officials who received them at Aden Adde International Airport in Mogadishu. EU-backed programme The EU-funded Voluntary Humanitarian Return programme has facilitated the return of more than 2,000 Somali migrants from Libya since August 2022. Additional charter flights are expected during the final quarter of 2026. The IOM says participation in the programme is voluntary and based on migrants making an informed decision to return. Counselling is provided before departure, while assistance after arrival is focused on family reunification and helping returnees rebuild their lives. The repeated repatriations highlight the continued challenges facing Somali migrants travelling through Libya, a major transit route for people attempting to reach Europe. Somali authorities and international partners have increasingly focused on encouraging safer migration choices while providing assistance to citizens who return from detention or difficult conditions abroad. Erdoğan’s 2011 visit recalled In remarks at the ceremony, Mr Abdullahi recalled Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s visit to Mogadishu in 2011, when Somalia was facing a severe famine alongside major security challenges. The visit was seen at the time as a significant expression of Türkiye’s engagement with Somalia and helped strengthen bilateral relations. “President Erdoğan came to Somalia in 2011, at a time when people were saying Somalia was a dangerous and insecure place. Since then, the Turkish government has stood by us,” Mr Abdullahi said. The 2011 visit came during a devastating drought and famine that affected millions of Somalis and prompted a major international humanitarian response. Since then, Türkiye and Somalia have expanded cooperation across a range of areas, including development, humanitarian assistance, infrastructure, education and security. The anniversary ceremony in Mogadishu underscored the depth of the relationship between the two countries and the continued emphasis both sides place on strengthening bilateral cooperation. somalia.content: Uganda Begins Withdrawal of Troops From Somalia After Nearly 20 Years Latest Headlines Uganda Begins Withdrawal of Troops From Somalia After Nearly 20 Years Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Ambitions Expose the Illusion of Its Neutral Mediation UN political mission ends in Somalia with no agreed replacement to handle election dispute Somalia Faces Security Vacuum as AU Troops Prepare to Leave Key Military Bases Ethiopia Says It Acquired 12 Russian Fighter Jets Amid Rising Tensions With Eritrea Advertise with us Home News Puntland Somalia World Sports Press Releases Somaliland Videos Opinion Contact Privacy Policy English Somali Uganda Begins Withdrawal of Troops From Somalia After Nearly 20 Years Staff Reporter GAROWE ONLINE Posted On 30-10-2026, 02:16PM MOGADISHU, Somalia — Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement, marking a significant development in the African Union's security mission as financial pressures and shifting international support raise questions about its future. Uganda's Chief of Defence Forces, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, announced the start of the withdrawal Thursday, saying the country was handing over security responsibilities to Somali forces. "As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," Kainerugaba wrote on X on Oct. 29. The announcement comes as the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, known as AUSSOM, faces growing financial and logistical challenges following changes in international funding arrangements. According to Uganda's Daily Monitor, the withdrawal comes amid a 25% reduction in funding from the United Nations Support Office in Somalia and uncertainty over continued U.S. support for the mission. Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni had previously defended the deployment, saying Uganda's involvement was driven by regional security interests and solidarity with neighboring countries. Speaking at a summit of troop-contributing countries in Kampala on July 31, Museveni said Somalia would not be abandoned even if international partners withdrew their support. "If the international community wants to pull out, let them. ... Somalia will not be abandoned. We have the capacity," he said. The financial difficulties have also raised concerns about the sustainability of AUSSOM, which relies heavily on international assistance for essential logistical support, including food, fuel, medical services and transportation. The United States had indicated in July that it would not support renewing the mission's mandate at the United Nations Security Council in December. However, Washington later agreed to give the U.N. an additional 12 months to wind down its logistical support, with the drawdown expected to begin in January 2027. Uganda was the first country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) in 2007 and has maintained one of the largest military contingents in the country. Over the years, Ugandan forces have fought alongside the Somali National Army in operations against al-Shabab, helping secure strategic towns and protect key government installations. AMISOM was replaced by the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) in 2022, which was subsequently succeeded by AUSSOM in 2025. The current mission is tasked with supporting Somali security forces, protecting civilians and facilitating the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to national institutions. The African Union has pledged to continue supporting Somalia despite the funding challenges. African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf said the bloc would mobilize political, diplomatic and financial assistance to support the country's security transition. The beginning of Uganda's withdrawal raises questions about the future composition of the African Union force and Somalia's ability to assume greater responsibility for national security as international support undergoes significant changes. Tensions in the Horn of Africa The comments come amid renewed diplomatic and political tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, prompting concerns over the potential impact on security and stability across the Horn of Africa. Relations between the two neighbours have deteriorated amid disagreements over regional security and competing political interests. The two countries fought a devastating border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. Their relationship has since faced renewed strains over developments in the region. Somalia maintains diplomatic relations with both Ethiopia and Eritrea and has repeatedly emphasised dialogue and regional cooperation as ways of addressing disputes. Mr Hassan Sheikh’s latest remarks reinforce Mogadishu’s stated policy of avoiding involvement in the Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute while maintaining working relations with both governments. He said Somalia would continue to prioritise peaceful relations and cooperation as part of wider efforts to support stability in the Horn of Africa. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Ethiopia reportedly plans to withdraw more than 3,000 troops from Somalia Posted by: Horseed Staff Ethiopia is reportedly preparing to withdraw more than 3,000 troops from neighbouring Somalia as renewed fighting inside Ethiopia puts pressure on the government to redirect military resources towards conflicts at home. 30 October, 2026 Share Tweet The reported plan has not been publicly confirmed by the Ethiopian or Somali governments, or by the African Union. A Somali Defence Ministry official told Bloomberg that Mogadishu had received no notification from Addis Ababa about a possible withdrawal. “Ethiopia has not informed us of any plan to withdraw its troops from Somalia,” the official said. It remains unclear how many troops would ultimately leave, which deployments would be affected or whether Somali forces or other personnel serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) would take over their positions. Uncertainty over Ethiopian deployments Ethiopia maintains troops in Somalia under different arrangements. Some Ethiopian forces serve as part of AUSSOM, the African Union mission supporting Somali security forces in operations against al-Shabab. Others are deployed under separate bilateral security arrangements with Mogadishu. As a result, it is not yet clear whether the reported withdrawal would affect one category of forces or both. Ethiopia has maintained a significant military presence in Somalia for years and has played an important role in operations against al-Shabab. AUSSOM said in September that an Ethiopian contingent had completed a troop rotation in Sector Four, with new personnel replacing soldiers who had completed a three-year deployment. The incoming forces were expected to continue working alongside Somali security forces on security and stabilisation operations. Fighting intensifies inside Ethiopia The reported withdrawal comes as Ethiopia faces renewed armed conflict in parts of the country. Fighting has intensified in the northern Tigray region, while insecurity involving armed groups has also continued elsewhere. The developments are putting additional pressure on Ethiopia’s military resources and could influence the country’s ability to maintain deployments beyond its borders. Ethiopia has previously redeployed troops from Somalia during periods of intensified fighting at home, including during the Tigray conflict. The latest reported plan could therefore mark a shift in Addis Ababa’s military priorities if it goes ahead. Potential implications for Somalia Any substantial withdrawal could affect security arrangements in parts of Somalia where Ethiopian forces have operated for years. Ethiopian troops have been involved in operations against al-Shabab and have maintained positions in several areas, including parts of southern and central Somalia. A significant reduction in their presence could require Somali forces or other AUSSOM contingents to assume additional responsibilities. However, the scale and timing of any withdrawal remain uncertain. Neither Addis Ababa nor Mogadishu has formally announced a troop pullout, and the African Union has not publicly announced a change to Ethiopia’s AUSSOM deployment. For now, the reported plan remains subject to confirmation, with key questions still unanswered over which Ethiopian forces could leave Somalia and whether replacements would be deployed. football.summary: أسفرت قرعة دور المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا عن تشكيل مجموعة قوية للهلال السوداني، حيث انضم إلى المجموعة الرابعة التي تضم بيراميدز المصري وحوريا كوناكري الغيني والمغرب الفاسي. يعتبر الهلال السوداني من الأندية العريقة في أفريقيا، ويأمل في تحقيق نتائج إيجابية في هذه البطولة. في سياق متصل، حقق الهلال فوزاً على إيغل نوار بهدفين في مباراة سابقة ضمن البطولة، مما يعزز من معنويات الفريق قبل انطلاق دور المجموعات. كما شهدت الساحة الرياضية السودانية بعض الأحداث المثيرة، حيث انتقد صحفي سوداني إدارة نادي المريخ بعد خروج الفريق من المنافسات، بينما أكد موقع مصري تأهل المريخ للمجموعات. يتطلع عشاق كرة القدم في السودان إلى أداء مميز من الهلال في هذه النسخة من البطولة.
